systems.name: The Real, Compleat M-Lode Taxonomy System
systems.summary: The M-Lode system is a closed, finite classification of all guitar chord voicings organized into families defined by interval content. It pairs 3-part and 4-part structural counterparts: Triads with 7th Chords, 7th-no-3rd with TBN I, 7th-no-5th with TBN II, 3-Part 4ths with 4-Part 4ths, and 3-Part Spread Clusters with 4-Part Spread Clusters. The system is finite because Spread Clusters supply the missing link that closes the taxonomy. Within the system, interval omissions occur only inside three specific 3-part families (triads, 3-part 4ths, spread clusters), while four families (7th no-3rd, 7th no-5th, TBN I, TBN II) exhibit the most balanced interval distribution across both 3- and 4-part voicings.

members.name: Triads (3-part)
members.summary: Primarily 3rds and 6ths with some 4ths and 5ths; no 2nds or 7ths.

members.name: 7th Chords (4-part)
members.summary: 4-part counterpart of triads in the M-Lode pairing.

members.name: 7th Chord No-3rd (3-part)
members.summary: 7th chord with the 3rd omitted; one of the two triadic subtypes derivable from a 4-part 7th chord.

members.name: TBN I (4-part)
members.summary: 4-part counterpart of 7th-no-3rd; exhibits even interval distribution across both voicing densities.

members.name: 7th Chord No-5th (3-part)
members.summary: 7th chord with the 5th omitted; the second triadic subtype derivable from a 4-part 7th chord.

members.name: TBN II (4-part)
members.summary: 4-part counterpart of 7th-no-5th; exhibits even interval distribution across both voicing densities.

members.name: 3-Part 4th Voicings
members.summary: Primarily 4ths and 5ths with some 2nds and 7ths; no 3rds or 6ths.

members.name: 4-Part 4th Voicings
members.summary: 4-part counterpart of 3-part 4ths in the M-Lode pairing.

members.name: 3-Part Spread Clusters
members.summary: Named by literal pitch content (e.g., C D E) rather than chord symbol.

members.name: 4-Part Spread Clusters
members.summary: The missing structural link that completes and closes the entire M-Lode taxonomy.

traversal_rules.name: 3-Part / 4-Part Family Pairing Navigation
traversal_rules.summary: Move between chord families by following the M-Lode's paired 3-part / 4-part counterpart structure: each 3-part family maps to exactly one 4-part family.

references.quote_excerpt: So, the REAL, COMPLEAT M-LODE depiction is: 3-Part Structures 4-Part Structures

traversal_rules.name: Four-Family Even-Distribution Symmetry
traversal_rules.summary: When moving across voicing density (3-part to 4-part or vice versa), prefer the four families with even interval distribution: 7th no-3rd, 7th no-5th, TBN I, TBN II.

references.quote_excerpt: the four chord families with the most even distribution are found both in 3- and 4-part chords

modification_rules.name: Interval Omission Restricted to Three Families
modification_rules.summary: Interval omission is permitted only within triads, 3-part 4ths, and spread clusters.

references.quote_excerpt: the omission of interval types only occurs within particular 3-part chord families (triad; 3-part 4th; spread cluster)

modification_rules.name: Spread Cluster Literal-Pitch Naming Rule
modification_rules.summary: Name 3-part spread clusters by their literal pitch content (e.g., 'C D E') rather than forcing them into a chord symbol.

references.quote_excerpt: Just name it like it is! Call it C D E!

modification_rules.name: Sus4 Notation Rule for Stacked-Fourth Chords
modification_rules.summary: Stacked-fourth chords (3-part and 4-part) must be labelled using sus4 notation rather than complex alterations or shorthand like C2.

references.quote_excerpt: My suggestion for a suitable name for this chord would be: G [sus4].

systems.name: Voice-Reduction Derivation System
systems.summary: The derivation system is the method's central generative procedure: smaller chord structures are produced by systematically omitting one voice from a larger parent chord. Each 4-part parent family generates a characteristic set of 3-part children via drop procedures (Drop 2, Drop 3, Drop 2&3, Drop 2&4, Double Drop 2 Drop 3) applied across root position and inversions. Every 3-part chord type appears inside exactly four different 4-part families, creating a cross-family reharmonization lattice.

members.name: Parent: TBN I (4-part)
members.summary: Source for Drop 2, Drop 3, Drop 2&3, Drop 2&4, Double Drop 2 Drop 3 derivations.

members.name: Parent: TBN II (4-part)
members.summary: Source for the same drop procedures across root and inversions.

members.name: Parent: 4-Part 4th Chord
members.summary: Generates 3-part 4ths by no-5th and no-3rd omissions.

traversal_rules.name: Four-Family Symmetry Reharmonization Rule
traversal_rules.summary: Because each 3-part chord type appears in exactly four different 4-part families, substitute any of the four parent families when harmonizing a given 3-part sonority.

modification_rules.name: Voice Omission Derivation Procedure
modification_rules.summary: Reduce a 4-part chord to a 3-part chord by omitting exactly one voice; the choice of omitted voice determines the resulting 3-part family.

references.quote_excerpt: a brief, introductory study of how to arrive at different 3-part chords by leaving out one voice of a 4-part chord

modification_rules.name: Density Floor: Three-Voice Minimum
modification_rules.summary: The derivation procedure produces 3-part chords as its floor; further reduction below three parts is not part of the M-Lode derivation system.

references.quote_excerpt: 3-part chords are easier to play than 4-part chords. Also, they often afford more space between the voices for melodic embellishment.

modification_rules.name: Grip-Slipping Inversion Cycle
modification_rules.summary: Cycle through all inversions of a chord type using Drop 3 voicings within a whole-tone (six tonic) system; extendable to Drop 2 and Drop 2&4.

references.quote_excerpt: a series of exercises...to help them learn all the inversions of different chords...The voicing type is Drop 3.

systems.name: Diatonic and Chromatic Voice-Leading Application System
systems.summary: This system governs how the M-Lode voicings are moved through harmonic progressions. It operates over five parent scales (C Major, C Melodic Minor, C Harmonic Minor, C Harmonic Major, C Hungarian Minor) and distinguishes Generic Diatonic Voice-Leading (GDVL) from Specific Chromatic Voice-Leading (SCVL). Within GDVL, voice-leading patterns are analysed through abstract A-B-C labels that classify intervallic motion separately from functional motion (tracked by the M.S.R.P. sequence). Six possible generic voice-leading patterns exist; prior volumes used only three. The governing aesthetic is that melody and harmony are structural equals.

traversal_rules.name: Diatonic Scale Transposition Expectation
traversal_rules.summary: All material presented in C Major must be transposed to C Melodic Minor, C Harmonic Minor, C Harmonic Major, and C Hungarian Minor.

references.quote_excerpt: The assumption is that our readers will have (by now) developed the necessary skills to make the needed adjustments to change the material to other 7-note scales.
We present it in 5 scales: 1. C Major 2. C Melodic Minor 3. C Harmonic Minor 4. C Harmonic Major 5. C Hungarian Minor

traversal_rules.name: Generic Voice-Leading Pattern Selection (6-Pattern Space)
traversal_rules.summary: When sequencing chords through a scale, select one of six possible generic voice-leading patterns encoded as A-B-C cycles; the three new alternates introduced in this volume should also be explored.

references.topic: Only 3 generic VLs used in Vols I & II
references.quote_excerpt: Note: Only 3 different generic voice-leadings were used out of 6!

traversal_rules.name: Intervallic vs. Functional Motion Analysis (M.S.R.P.)
traversal_rules.summary: Distinguish intervallic motion (interval size per voice) from functional motion (chord-tone strand assignment tracked by the M.S.R.P. sequence).

traversal_rules.name: Melody-Harmony Equality Aesthetic Rule
traversal_rules.summary: Voice-leading choices must treat melodic and harmonic motion as structural equals; subordinating either is a departure from the method's governing aesthetic.

references.quote_excerpt: excellent voice-leading treats both melody and harmony as equals.

modification_rules.name: GDVL-to-SCVL Mode Switch
modification_rules.summary: Switch from Generic Diatonic to Specific Chromatic voice-leading when using Drop 3 voicings in a whole-tone (Grip-Slipping) context or when crossing diatonic scale boundaries.

references.quote_excerpt: The IVLs and the FVLs are all examples of SCVL (specific chromatic voice-leading), as opposed to GDVL (generic diatonic voice-leading), which is all of Volumes 1 & 2.

modification_rules.name: Duet Texture with Passing Tones
modification_rules.summary: Split a 4-part voicing into two two-voice duets (top two / bottom two) and add passing tones; especially effective in harmonic minor.

references.topic: Duet texture with passing tones instruction
references.quote_excerpt: 4-part; no passing tones Duet (top 2, bottom 2); add p.t.. NICE in Harmonic minor!

modification_rules.name: Harmonic Major b6 Substitution
modification_rules.summary: Modify any C Major voicing by substituting Ab for A (b6), converting the material to Harmonic Major without changing the underlying voice-leading structure.

references.quote_excerpt: just play Ab (b6) instead of A (6). There are nearly 200 pages to explore!

modification_rules.name: Hungarian Minor #4 Substitution
modification_rules.summary: Modify any Harmonic Minor passage by raising the 4th by a semitone (#4), converting the material to Hungarian Minor.

references.quote_excerpt: Hungarian Minor...a harmonic minor scale with #4..
